To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the chemical reaction is able to sustain the propagation of the reaction front, (2) the buoyancy instability can be suppressed by a sufficiently strong chemical reaction and (3) the growth rate of the instability is reduced with the increase in chemical reaction rate.

we have developed a new approach for the study of the Rayleigh–Taylor instability of miscible fluid interfaces in the presence of chemical reaction and that we have shown that this instability is responsible for the observed buoyant instability of the reaction front in Hele-Shaw cells.

the growth rates of a chemical reaction front in a thin cell is well described by the Rayleigh-Taylors instability of two miscible fluids, which is modified by the buoyancy of the reacted fluid and the reaction front velocity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the stability and the dynamics of chemical waves in thin Hele-Shaw cells, where buoyancy effects are important.
the dynamics of the interface between a miscible and an immiscible fluid.
the study of the Rayleigh–Taylor instability of a miscible fluid in a Hele–Shaw cell.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the instability of the front is due to buoyancy and the chemical reaction.
the chemical reaction is able to stabilize the instability in a Hele- Shaw cell, and the buoyant instability of the interface is able to destabilize the chemical reaction.
our model is able to reproduce the observed instability in terms of its linear growth rate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the instability is a consequence of the combined action of the buoyancy and the chemical reaction.
the buoyant instability of the reaction front is due to the combined effect of the reaction and the buoyancy.
the buoyant Rayleigh-Taylor (RT) instability of the interface is enhanced by a reaction front, while the reaction front is stabilized by the buoyancy of the interface.
The main takeaway from our work is that
chemical reactions can have a profound influence on the evolution of miscible fluids.
the instability is not only driven by density differences but also by a concentration difference between the reacting fluids.
the chemical reaction does not alter the instability mechanism.
